passage: Akash sir said the legs of my cow were too short. I had worked on that cow all morning. My face went hot and I said, "Then the whole drawing is bad." I put my head on the desk. He did not get cross. He said, "I did not say the drawing is bad. I said the legs are short." Then he gave me an eraser and asked me to measure the legs against the body with my pencil. I did not want to, but I did it. The legs got longer. The cow stood up better. I still felt a little bit sad. Sarita

qa.q: What did Akash sir say was wrong with the cow?
qa.a: Akash sir said the legs of the cow were too short.

qa.q: Why did Sarita say the whole drawing was bad?
qa.a: Sarita felt hurt and ashamed, as if the correction about the legs meant the whole cow and the morning's work were judged.

qa.q: What helped Sarita move from putting the head down to fixing the drawing?
qa.a: Akash sir stayed calm, said only the legs were short, and gave an eraser and a way to measure the legs against the body.

qa.q: How does Akash sir see the short legs?
qa.a: Akash sir sees them as one part of the drawing to fix and not a judgment of the drawing or of Sarita.

grounding: Shows a child feeling the whole self judged after a correction, and a teacher separating the fix from the worth of the child.

passage: Note from class teacher, Friday. During spelling correction today, Deepak received his notebook with "recieve" marked wrong. He pushed the book away and said the teacher's board was wrong. He crossed his arms and would not look up. I did not argue. I sat beside him and showed him the word in the dictionary, then asked him to find it himself. He did, quietly. Then I told him one wrong letter does not cancel the four he got right on that line. He wrote the word three times. He asked if he could keep the eraser. Please praise the four correct spellings at home before the fifth. Himani, class teacher

qa.q: Which word was marked wrong in Deepak's notebook?
qa.a: The word "recieve" was marked wrong in Deepak's notebook.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he pushed the book away and crossed his arms?
qa.a: Deepak felt hurt and defensive, and his claim that the board was wrong shows the mistake stung him.

qa.q: What could Deepak's parents do at home to support him after this?
qa.a: They could first praise what he got right in his spelling and then look at the one wrong letter with him calmly, without turning it into a judgment of him.

qa.q: How does Himani see Deepak's reaction?
qa.a: Himani sees it as hurt more than defiance, which is why the teacher sat beside him, used a dictionary and pointed out the four correct letters.

grounding: Shows a child crumpling and arguing after correction, and a teacher patiently separating one mistake from the child's worth.

passage: In a primary school in Addis Ababa, Abebe, eight, handed in his map of Ethiopia with rivers drawn in bright blue. His teacher, Ms Nadia, put a small red circle on one river. "This one flows the other way, Abebe." His face crumpled. He grabbed the map back. "It's all wrong! I'm bad at maps!" He pushed it under his desk. Ms Nadia knelt beside him. "Abebe, the map is lovely. One river goes the wrong way. You're not wrong; one line is." He sniffed, not convinced. She showed him the river on the big wall map. After a while, he rubbed out the arrow and drew it the other way, still sulking a little.

qa.q: What colour were the rivers on Abebe's map?
qa.a: The rivers were drawn in bright blue.

qa.q: Why did Abebe say he was bad at maps?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed, taking the one red circle as a judgment of himself rather than of one line.

qa.q: What did Ms Nadia do that helped?
qa.a: She knelt beside him, praised the map and separated the one wrong line from him, then showed the river on the wall map.

qa.q: How might Ms Nadia feel when Abebe crumples?
qa.a: Ms Nadia might feel concerned and gentle, understanding that a small correction felt huge to him.

grounding: Shows a child who feels his whole self is judged when one part of his map is corrected, and a teacher separating work from worth.

passage: In the school art room, Vandana, eleven, showed her painting of a sunset to her art teacher, Keerthana ma'am. "The colours are lovely," ma'am said. "But the trees are floating. Let's give them roots on the ground." Vandana's eyes filled. "You always find something wrong! I'm never good at anything." She turned away and started packing her brushes. Keerthana ma'am waited, then said quietly, "Vandana, I'd only bother correcting a painting worth fixing. The trees are one thing. You're the one who mixed that orange." Vandana wiped her face with her sleeve. After a minute, she took the brush out again and painted a thin brown line under each tree.

qa.q: What was Vandana's painting of?
qa.a: It was a painting of a sunset.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when she said she was never good at anything?
qa.a: She felt hurt and discouraged, taking a correction about the trees as a judgment of her whole self.

qa.q: What did Keerthana ma'am say that helped Vandana return to the painting?
qa.a: She separated the one fix from Vandana's worth, pointing out that the painting was worth correcting and praising the orange she mixed.

qa.q: How might Keerthana ma'am feel when Vandana picks up the brush again?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and warm, seeing Vandana try again after the hurt passed.

grounding: Shows a child who feels a correction as a judgment of her whole self and a teacher helping her separate the work from her worth.

passage:
Monday. Anjali, nine, wrote a story about a lost puppy. Her mother Seema read it and said, "Nice! Just check the spelling of 'because'." Anjali snatched the page. "Then it's rubbish!" She ran to her room and slammed the door.
Wednesday. Seema tried again, differently. "I love your puppy's name. Can I show you one word that's playing tricks?" Anjali looked, frowned, and fixed it herself, without a word.
Saturday. Anjali brought a new story to her mother. "Can you check if there are any tricky words? But say the good part first." Seema laughed and said the ending made her cry. Then she pointed to two words. Anjali corrected them, humming.

qa.q: What was Anjali's first story about?
qa.a: It was about a lost puppy.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling on Monday when she snatched the page?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset, hearing one spelling correction as proof that the whole story was rubbish.

qa.q: What changed in Seema's approach, and why did it help?
qa.a: She started with what she loved and called the error a tricky word, which separated the mistake from Anjali's worth.

qa.q: How does Seema feel by Saturday?
qa.a: Seema feels happy and amused, laughing when Anjali asks for the good part first and corrects words while humming.

grounding: Shows over a week a child who first feels a correction as a judgment of herself, then learns to accept it with kind repetition.

passage: "Dilnaz, come, leave that torn page. Let your Nani Farida tell you something. When I was nine, my Khala taught me embroidery. I made a parrot on a handkerchief and I was so proud. Khala looked and said, 'The tail stitches are too loose.' I threw the hoop on the floor and shouted, 'Then everything I make is rubbish!' I cried under the stairs all afternoon. Next day Khala sat with me, unpicked just three stitches and said, 'The stitch was wrong. You were not.' I didn't believe her for a long time. It took many parrots and many gentle corrections before a red mark stopped feeling like a slap. Now show me the sum your teacher marked. Just the sum."

qa.q: What did young Farida embroider on the handkerchief?
qa.a: A parrot.

qa.q: What was young Farida feeling when Khala pointed at the tail stitches?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, as if her whole self had been judged, so she threw the hoop and cried under the stairs.

qa.q: What did Khala do the next day that became a turning point?
qa.a: Khala sat beside her, unpicked only three stitches and separated the stitch from the child: "The stitch was wrong. You were not."

qa.q: How might Khala have felt when the hoop hit the floor?
qa.a: Khala was probably surprised and sorry to see the child so hurt, which may be why she came back gently the next day.

grounding: Shows a child who takes a correction of her embroidery as a judgement of her whole self, and learns slowly through kind repetition to separate the work from her worth.
